newsitem.title: USA: Danish actress fights to get baby back in New York.
newsitem.headline: Danish actress fights to get baby back in New York.

text.p: A Danish woman who temporarily left her baby outside a New York restaurant fought on Wednesday to get the child back from city foster care, but her efforts were slowed by bureaucratic and legal technicalities.

The 14-month-old girl was taken from Danish actress Annette Sorensen, 30, on Saturday after she was left in a stroller parked outside the window of an East Village restaurant. Sorenson and the baby's father, an American, were inside having a drink, police said.
Sorensen's attorneys claimed such a practice was common in Copenhagen, but officials questioned the wisdom of transplanting such trust to the streets of New York.
"Leaving a child unattended on a city street for an hour in New York seems to me pretty inappropriate," said Nicholas Scoppetta, head of the city's Administration of Children's Services.
Passers-by who noticed the baby outside the restaurant said she was cold and crying and called police.

The child welfare agency placed Liv Sorensen in foster care after her mother and her father, Exavier Wardlaw of Brooklyn, were arrested on charges of endangering the welfare of a child and disorderly conduct.
But such an incident "would never happen in Denmark," Michael Dyrby, an editor of Denmark's TV2 Denmark, told CNN.
"It happens all the time you have your child with you that you leave them outside a restaurant or outside of a shop," he said.
"In Denmark, it's very unusual that authorities interfere ... in family matters," he said. "We consider that the mother knows what's best for the child."

A New York Family Court judge late on Tuesday ordered the baby returned to her mother, but procedural issues slowed the process, and the reunion was not likely until Thursday morning, authorities said.
"It's a logistical matter at this point," a spokeswoman for the welfare agency said.
The mother appeared angry as she left Family Court after a day of legal wrangling. She had already spent two days in jail.
Among other issues, plans for the mother and child to stay in the Danish Consulate were abandoned because of the need for social workers to visit, Scoppetta said.
Under the judge's order, the baby must never be left alone with Sorensen and another adult must always be present.
David Kirsch, the father's attorney, said Sorensen had been in the United States less than 48 hours when her daughter was taken from her.
She and Wardlaw are due in Criminal Court next Monday, and she must return to Family Court next week for a hearing on the custody of her child.
